name: Savanna
notes: Tropical grassland with scattered fire-adapted trees: continuous C4 grass layer under flat-crowned acacias, baobabs and palms. Drawn on the East African Serengeti/miombo, Brazilian Cerrado, Australian tropical savanna and Indian savanna-woodland.

canopy.name: African baobab

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling has broad cotyledons and simple, undivided first leaves; hand-shaped leaves with 3, then 5-7 leaflets come later. Young baobabs look nothing like adults: a slender, straight, tapering grey-green whip over a swollen tuberous taproot, with thin branches; the huge bottle trunk and wide crown form only after decades. Seeds are hard and germinate slowly unless scarified.
growth.source: Ethiopian Forestry Dev. baobab study (simple juvenile leaves, 5-7-foliate adult leaves, trees over 1000 yr); Anjarwalla et al. 2021 bioRxiv (seed-grown trees first flower at 8-23 yr; acid-treated seed sprouts in ~5 d); Patrut et al. 2018 Nature Plants (radiocarbon ages to ~2500 yr); height curve estimated

canopy.source: African savanna, Sahel to Limpopo. The upside-down tree; thousands of years old; hollow trunks shelter people and bees. All 8 Kew-accepted species. Deciduous in the dry season, bat-pollinated white flowers at night, fruit by mammals.

flower.form: big pendulous white flowers 15-20 cm with crumpled petals and a ball of stamens, opening at night, browning by morning

fruit.form: large egg-shaped pods 15-25 cm, velvety yellow-grey-brown, hanging on long stalks; chalky white pulp

appearance.seasonal: deciduous, bare for most of the dry season (8-9 months); leaves flush at the rains
appearance.silhouette: the upside-down tree: a vast grey bottle trunk with a spreading tangle of thick, stubby, root-like branches; leafless most of the year

fruiting.source: Venter & Witkowski 2019 For Ecol Manage (southern Africa: flowering 1-5 months peaking Nov, 290-710 flowers per tree, fruit set ~20%); EFD Ethiopia study (57-157 fruits/tree in Benin, 77 in South Africa); Baum 1995 (pendent white flowers open at dusk for one night, fruit-bat pollination)

canopy.name: Boab

growth.juvenile_note: The seedling forms a swollen, carrot-like (edible) tuberous root and simple, entire first leaves; compound leaves with 5-7 leaflets come later. Young boabs are thin, straight whips, often several-stemmed after fire or browsing; the bottle-shaped trunk swells slowly over decades and the tree drops its leaves each dry season.
growth.source: ANPSA (small spreading tree to ~12 m; the Kings Park boab estimated ~750 yr old); seed dormancy study in Seed Sci Res (hard seed); tuberous seedlings and simple juvenile leaves as in other baobabs; growth rate and first flowering estimated from A. digitata

canopy.source: Kimberley, NW Australia. Swollen bottle trunk; prison tree. All 8 Kew-accepted species. Deciduous in the dry season, bat-pollinated white flowers at night, fruit by mammals.

canopy.name: Miombo tree

traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

canopy.silhouette: flat spreading crown, short crooked trunk

growth.juvenile_note: Big flat seeds flung from exploding pods sprout within 1-3 weeks of the first rains. The seedling grows a deep taproot and woody rootstock; for years (often a decade or more) its leafy shoots of paired leaflets die back in the dry season or to fire and resprout, forming a low multi-stemmed tuft, until one shoot escapes as a single stem. New leaves flush wine-red before turning green.
growth.source: Wikipedia (16-19 m, grows very slowly, red to purple spring flush turning green in 10-20 d, pods 12-15 cm split explosively flinging 2 cm seeds); miombo regeneration literature (suffrutex/'gulliver' seedling stage, Chidumayo); timings and ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (small fragrant green flowers in racemes after the late-August leaf flush; flat woody pods 12-15 cm, mature from about April, split explosively); bee visitors from miombo honey literature; timings and counts estimated.

canopy.name: Umbrella thorn
canopy.origin: Africa (Sahel to South Africa) and Arabia

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal: two oval cotyledons, then tiny feathery bipinnate leaves on a thin stem with paired spines, some long, straight and white, others short and hooked. The taproot dives deep first. Browsed saplings become dense, low, cage-like spiny bushes for years; once a leader escapes browsers it gains about 1.5 m in two years and only later spreads the flat umbrella crown.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): up to 21 m, about 1.5 m in 2 years, a 6-7-year-old tree yields 5-6 kg of clean seed, 10-12 kg pods a year at 10 yr; Andersen & Krzywinski 2007 (BMC Ecology): radiocarbon ages of 200-650 yr for trees in Egypt's Eastern Desert, radial growth up to 2.4 mm a year. Germination and height curve estimated.

canopy.source: Sahel to South Africa savanna; the flat-top. Kew POWO (African acacias are now Vachellia/Senegalia; Acacia is the Australian wattles). Thorny (African), flat crowns, insect-pollinated, pods eaten by browsers which spread the seed; giraffe and goat browse; fire-adapted.

flower.form: small creamy-white fluffy balls in clusters

fruit.form: pale yellow-brown pods twisted into tight spirals and coils, 8-12 cm; fall for browsers

appearance.refs: Wikipedia Vachellia tortilis; Kew POWO; PlantZAfrica

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Acacia tortilis): white or pale yellowish-white heads 0.5-1.1 cm, pods 7-10 cm by 6-10 mm, spirally twisted, 10-12 kg pods per 10-yr tree; the Turkana make porridge from the pods, the Maasai eat immature seeds; Wikipedia: aromatic flowers, springlike coiled pods. Flowering at the onset of the rains, ripening, pod fall and rot times estimated.

canopy.soil_note: 1 Oct (Mike: acacias must be in the game): was the 'sand' preset, a hard gate to sand and sandstone only, so on alluvium or granite the savanna's acacia could not spawn at all. Vachellia tortilis grows on sandy, loamy, rocky and alluvial soils and tolerates salt; it avoids waterlogging (no clay_peat).

canopy.name: Marula
canopy.source: Sclerocarya birrea (A.Rich.) Hochst., marula, single-stemmed deciduous tree of African savanna and open woodland, 9-18 m, plum-sized yellow fruit (Kew POWO; Palgrave 2002 Trees of Southern Africa; ICRAF Agroforestree)
canopy.silhouette: rounded spreading crown on a mottled grey trunk

bark.notes: grey bark flaking in roundish patches to show paler brown under-bark, giving a mottled look

leaf.notes: pinnate leaves of 7-17 ovate pointed leaflets crowded at the branch tips

flower.form: small flowers with red sepals and white-yellow petals in spikes, male and female on separate trees

fruit.form: round plum-like drupe 3-4 cm, falling green and ripening pale yellow on the ground

appearance.seasonal: deciduous in the dry season; flowers with the new leaves
appearance.silhouette: rounded spreading crown on a mottled grey trunk
appearance.refs: Palgrave 2002; ICRAF Agroforestree Sclerocarya birrea; Kew POWO

growth.juvenile_note: The hard stone has lidded openings that pop off for the seedling, often after passing through an elephant. The seedling is a straight whip with pinnate leaves over a swollen taproot; it drops its leaves each dry season and grows into a single-stemmed tree with a rounded crown.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree (Sclerocarya birrea: to 18 m, fruiting from about 7 yr from seed); Palgrave 2002. Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree; Palgrave 2002 (dioecious; flowers Sep-Nov with new leaves; fruit Jan-Mar, falls green and ripens yellow on the ground; up to 500 kg per tree; eaten by elephants, people and many animals).

canopy.name: Sausage tree
canopy.source: Kigelia africana (Lam.) Benth., sausage tree, broad-crowned tree of African savanna, riverbanks and open woodland, 8-20 m, maroon night flowers and huge sausage fruits on long cords (Kew POWO; Palgrave 2002 Trees of Southern Africa; PlantZAfrica)
canopy.silhouette: broad dark crown hung with huge grey sausages on cords

bark.notes: smooth grey-brown bark, flaking in thin plates on old trunks

leaf.notes: rough pinnate leaves of 7-11 oblong leaflets, in whorls of three at the branch ends

flower.form: large velvety maroon cup flowers 10 cm on long dangling ropes, opening at night

fruit.form: grey-brown woody sausage 30-100 cm, up to 10 kg, hanging on a cord

appearance.seasonal: semi-deciduous in the dry season; flowers in late dry season
appearance.silhouette: broad dark crown hung with huge grey sausages on cords
appearance.refs: PlantZAfrica Kigelia africana; Palgrave 2002; Kew POWO

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds are freed when the woody fruit rots or is broken by elephants, hippos or baboons; the seedling is a straight whip with large rough pinnate leaves in whorls of three. It grows fairly fast into a single-trunked tree with a broad rounded crown.
growth.source: PlantZAfrica (fast-growing, flowers from 5-8 yr; bat-pollinated night flowers; fruit to 1 m and 10 kg); Palgrave 2002. Lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: PlantZAfrica; Palgrave 2002 (flowers on long pendulous panicles, open at night, bat-pollinated, also sunbirds; fruit set very low; raw fruit purgative/toxic to people, eaten by elephants, hippos and baboons).

canopy.name: Camel thorn

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal, with two thick oval cotyledons and grey-green feathery bipinnate leaves on a zigzag stem armed with pairs of large, swollen-based, white spines. The seedling pours its effort into a taproot that heads down toward groundwater (in old trees it may reach tens of metres) while the shoot grows slowly, so young plants are sparse, very spiny, grey-green bushes for years.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (Vachellia erioloba): 2 m shrub to 16 m tree, slow-growing, starts flowering at about 10 years, seeds take 4-6 weeks to germinate after a boiling-water soak, taproot can reach 60 m; ICRAF Agroforestree: flowers at about 10 yr, regular pod crops by 20 yr, crown to 18 m. Height curve and lifespan estimated.

canopy.name: Fever tree

growth.juvenile_note: Hot-water-soaked seed sprouts quickly; seedlings have two oval cotyledons, reach the two-leaf stage in 6-8 weeks and carry feathery bipinnate leaves and pairs of straight white spines. Young trees shoot up 1-1.5 m a year as slender single-stemmed whips, and the powdery greenish-yellow bark that names the tree shows early; the flat-topped crown spreads later.
growth.source: SANBI PlantZAfrica (Vachellia xanthophloea): 15-25 m, about 1.5 m a year under ideal conditions, seed soaked overnight in hot water, two-leaf stage 6-8 weeks after sowing, dappled shade below; ICRAF Agroforestree: 1-1.5 m a year. First flowering, lifespan and height curve estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two small oval cotyledons on a short succulent hypocotyl, then a single erect, 3-5-winged green spiny column with tiny short-lived leaves at the tip. Stays an unbranched spiny column for years (often sheltered in a bush), then branches from the top into ascending, jointed candelabra arms while the base becomes a grey woody trunk.
growth.source: Useful Tropical Plants (E. candelabrum to 12-20 m; fresh seed germinates readily; cuttings root readily); Wikipedia (E. ingens, the close southern candelabra species). Growth rate, first flowering and ages estimated from tree euphorbias.

fruiting.source: Estimated from E. ingens/E. candelabrum descriptions (Wikipedia; Useful Tropical Plants): greenish-yellow cyathia in threes on the rib edges near the stem tips in the dry season, visited by bees and other insects; 3-lobed capsule red turning purple, explosively dehiscent; latex highly toxic.

shrub.silhouette: thorny tangled shrub with pink-yellow lantern flowers

growth.juvenile_note: Hard seeds germinate after scarification by fire or animal guts; epigeal, with round cotyledons, then feathery bipinnate leaves like the adult. The seedling soon becomes a thorny, many-stemmed bush: prolific root suckers and coppice shoots throw up new stems around it, forming dense, impenetrable thickets that encroach on savanna grassland.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree Database Dichrostachys cinerea (to 7 m; medium-slow height growth; flowers Oct-Feb S Africa; pods to 100 x 15 mm, twisted, in intertwined clusters, ripe May-Sep; ~4 seeds per pod; seeds long-lived; vigorous coppicing and prolific root suckers); Wikipedia (thorns to 8 cm, bipinnate leaves)

fruiting.source: ICRAF/Wikipedia ('Chinese lantern' spikes 6-8 cm: sterile pink-lilac flowers above, fertile yellow ones below; Oct-Feb; mustard-brown twisted indehiscent pods to 10 cm in dense clusters, ripe May-Sep, eaten by livestock and game). Flower size is the spike length; insect pollinators, set and crop estimated.

growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree Ziziphus mucronata (shrub or tree to 10 m; flowers Oct-Feb; fruit persists into winter); Palgrave 2002. Ages estimated.

fruiting.source: Palgrave 2002; ICRAF (small yellow-green flowers in axillary clusters, Oct-Feb; shiny red-brown fruit Mar-Aug, often persisting after leaf-fall, edible but mealy).

Delile, desert date (the trim seed list's 'Wild pomegranate' is Burchellia bubalina, a different plant), spiny evergreen shrub or small tree of Sahelian and East African savanna, 3-10 m (Kew POWO; Hall & Walker 1991 Balanites aegyptiaca monograph; ICRAF Agroforestree)
shrub.silhouette: tangled spiny grey-green crown with drooping tips

Browsed young plants become dense spiny bushes; protected ones grow a short trunk with a tangled crown of drooping green thorny twigs.

fruiting.source: Hall & Walker 1991; ICRAF (fragrant yellow-green flowers in the dry season; edible date-like drupes). Counts estimated.

shrub.name: Mopane
shrub.source: Colophospermum mopane (J.Kirk ex Benth.) J.Leonard, mopane, gregarious tree or multi-stemmed shrub forming mopane scrub on hot low-lying alkaline clays of southern African savanna, 2-10 m as scrub (to 18 m on deep soil) (Kew POWO; Palgrave 2002; Timberlake 1995 Mopane woodland)

fruiting.source: Palgrave 2002 (inconspicuous green flowers Dec-Mar; flat indehiscent kidney-shaped pods Apr-Jun, seed sticky with resin). Pollination and counts estimated.

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings are grassy tufts of thin tillers with lance-shaped leaves, well developed in 4 months. It flowers once, after 7-21 years, then the clump dies.

ground.silhouette: tussock with tangled twisted black awns

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings appear with the first big rains, often from seeds that drilled themselves into the soil with their hygroscopic twisting awns: a flat, bluish-green tuft of folded leaves that tillers into a loose tussock during its first wet season. Mature culms carry dark spikes whose long brown awns twist and tangle together into the typical 'tanglehead'.
growth.source: Tropical Forages factsheet (Heteropogon contortus: seed dormancy up to ~12 months, germination optimum 30-35 C, fertile tillers 0.5-1.5 m, tolerates light shade, flowers from late January in the south); NSW DPIRD GrassedUp (relatively short-lived perennial, growth starts with first rains); timings estimated.

ground.name: Giant termite mushroom
ground.source: Termitomyces titanicus Pegler & Piearce, giant termite mushroom, the largest edible mushroom, symbiont of Macrotermes termites in miombo woodland and savanna of Zambia, DR Congo and West Africa (Pegler & Piearce 1980 Kew Bulletin; Index Fungorum)
ground.silhouette: a giant grey-brown parasol on a termite mound

cap.form: huge flat grey-brown cap up to 1 m across with a dark pointed central umbo, splitting at the rim
cap.notes: the world's largest edible mushroom, rising from a termite nest on a thick stalk with a long root (pseudorrhiza) running down into the fungus comb

appearance.habit: single or few on and around termite mounds after the first heavy rains
appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain then rots (soft) or persists (woody brackets)
appearance.silhouette: a giant grey-brown parasol on a termite mound
appearance.refs: Pegler & Piearce 1980 Kew Bull. 35: 475; Wikipedia Termitomyces titanicus

repro.note: The mycelium is the organism and lives in the substrate for years; the mushroom is a days-long fruiting body. 'rhizome' here = the mycelium spreading through connected dead wood or litter; 'wind' = spores.

cap.notes: looks like a shaggy ink cap that never opens; dries hard and stands for months

underside.type: none; powdery brown spores inside the head

appearance.habit: single or scattered on bare sandy ground and termite mounds after rain
appearance.seasonal: fruits after rain then rots (soft) or persists (woody brackets)
appearance.silhouette: shaggy white clubs standing on bare sand

ground.name: Guinea grass
ground.source: Megathyrsus maximus (Jacq.) B.K.Simon & S.W.L.Jacobs (syn. Panicum maximum), Guinea grass, tall tufted grass of African savanna and woodland, common under trees, 1-3 m (Kew POWO: native tropical and southern Africa; Tropical Forages; FAO grassland index)
ground.silhouette: tall leafy tussock with wide open purplish panicles

leaf.notes: long flat blades up to 3.5 cm wide with a pale midrib

flower.form: large open panicle 15-50 cm with whorled lower branches, purplish when young

appearance.seasonal: green in the rains, straw and dry-season dormant
appearance.silhouette: tall leafy tussock with wide open purplish panicles

growth.juvenile_note: Seed (often dormant for months after shedding) gives a small tuft of flat blades; tillers multiply from the base and short rhizomes, and by the end of the first rains it is a dense leafy tussock 1-2 m tall sending up wide open panicles. It tolerates the shade of savanna trees better than most grasses.
growth.source: Tropical Forages Megathyrsus maximus (tufted perennial 0.5-3 m; seed dormancy; short-day flowering in many accessions; shade tolerant); Kew POWO.

ground.name: Fire lily
ground.source: Gloriosa superba, flame lily, tendril-climbing savanna herb across Africa/Asia, 0.5-3 m — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Gloriosa superba, flame lily, tendril-climbing savanna herb across Africa/Asia, 0
traits.trunk: long woody or soft climbing stem on a host
traits.note: leaf/trunk/petiole derived from the plant's shape class; per-species detail where the entry carries it (aroids, cannabis)

ground.silhouette: tendril climber with red-yellow flame flowers

growth.juvenile_note: Seedlings come up slowly and erratically (1-6 months); the first season often makes only a short unbranched shoot with a few glossy lance-shaped leaves and a pea-sized tuber. Each year the finger-like tuber grows and forks, sending up a longer, weak stem that climbs by tendril-like leaf tips through shrubs, then dies back to the tuber in the dry season.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Gloriosa superba: climbing stems to 4 m from a fleshy tuberous rhizome; highly toxic, colchicine). Germination time, tuber-building years and ages estimated from Gloriosa cultivation.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (solitary flowers with 6 reflexed wavy tepals 5-7.6 cm, red to orange with yellowish bases; likely pollinated by butterflies and sunbirds; fleshy capsule 6-12 cm with red seeds; all parts poisonous). Monsoon season, timings and counts estimated.

ground.restored_note: 1 Oct §CE (Mike: these plants must be in the game): restored after the §CC trim, which ran before the always_keep rule existed.

epiphyte.name: Leopard orchid

growth.juvenile_note: Starts as a dust-like seed that must meet a fungus; it swells into a tiny green protocorm on bark, then a thread of roots and one or two narrow strap leaves. Over years it builds a clump of upright, yellow, cane-like pseudobulbs (to 60 cm) with 6-7 pleated strap leaves near the top, ringed by a basket of stiff, upward-pointing white aerial roots that trap leaf litter.
growth.source: Wikipedia (Ansellia africana: robust clumps, some estimated over a tonne; yellow cane-like pseudobulbs to 60 cm with 6-7 leathery plicate leaves; upward-pointing white aerial roots forming a litter basket; panicles to 85 cm with 10-100 fragrant flowers 6 cm across, each lasting up to ~10 days). Germination, growth and ages estimated from orchid biology.

repro.note: dust seed by wind; germinates only where its fungus lives (reads mycorrhizal presence); most species need one specific pollinator

epiphyte.source: African savanna woodland. Big epiphyte clumps in savanna trees. Kew POWO.

leaf.notes: clump of tall ribbed pseudobulb canes 60 cm with pleated straps; upward-pointing spiky white aerial roots make a litter basket

epiphyte.name: Savanna ruffle lichen
epiphyte.source: Parmotrema austrosinense (Zahlbr.) Hale, a foliose ruffle lichen of sunny bark in warm-temperate and tropical savanna and woodland, including East and southern Africa, rosettes to 10 cm (Index Fungorum; Brodo, Sharnoff & Sharnoff 2001; Hale 1965)
epiphyte.silhouette: pale grey leafy rosettes on acacia bark

leaf.notes: broad rounded pale mineral-grey lobes with powdery soralia along the rims, black underside with a brown margin; rosettes to 10 cm

appearance.silhouette: pale grey leafy rosettes on acacia bark
appearance.refs: Brodo et al. 2001 Lichens of North America; Index Fungorum

growth.juvenile_note: Starts from a soredium caught in a bark crack: a pale dot that spreads outward as a ring of broad rounded lobes, a few millimetres a year, to a grey rosette a hand across with powdery rims.
growth.source: Brodo et al. 2001 (P. austrosinense: thallus to 10 cm, sorediate, on bark in warm regions); growth rate and ages estimated from foliose Parmeliaceae.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators
